text:
## 1. What fragrance is
A fine fragrance is a formulated mixture of odorants and supporting materials in a delivery matrix. A perfume concentrate may contain natural extracts, individual aroma chemicals, reconstructed accords, solvents or other functional materials. A finished fragrance may use ethanol/water, oil or another carrier. A perceived note can arise from several materials; a listed note is not an ingredient declaration or proof of origin. An accord is an olfactory impression produced by a combination of materials. A formula specifies materials, quantities and processing and may be commercially confidential. A fragrance family describes the dominant impression; one fragrance may span several families.

Top/opening, heart and base/drydown are descriptive stages rather than an exact stopwatch. Components evaporate, partition and interact at different rates; some are detectable through multiple stages. A linear fragrance changes relatively little perceptually; this does not mean it has no volatile materials. A fragrance can be complex without many advertised notes. Minimalist formulas can be sophisticated.

## 2. Concentration and performance
Common commercial ranges for ethanol-based fine fragrances are approximately cologne 3–8%, EDT 5–15%, EDP 10–20%, extrait/parfum 15–40%; ranges overlap and are not universal legal definitions. The word cologne can also denote a fresh citrus-aromatic style. Never infer an exact percentage from a category name. Ask whether a stated percentage is w/w, v/v, or another specified basis and whether it refers to the finished product or a premix. Do not compare numbers without compatible bases. See IFRA Transparency List FAQ. A high concentration is not automatically higher quality, safer, louder, longer-lasting or better value. Composition, dose, delivery, volatility, carrier, substrate, temperature, environment and individual perception matter. A perfume oil may project differently from a spray, but no universal ranking applies. Sillage = trail in air; projection = perceived reach from source; longevity = duration detectable under specified conditions; substantivity = persistence on a substrate; diffusion = spread in the environment. 'Beast mode', 'skin scent' and 'compliment getter' are informal consumer language, not measured specifications. Olfactory adaptation can reduce perceived intensity; other people may still notice it. Do not suggest repeated application solely to overcome adaptation. Ask about context and label usage instead.

## 3. Olfactory map and customer language
A practical map inspired by established fragrance classification, without reproducing a proprietary database or wheel. Family boundaries differ by classification system. These descriptors are tendencies, not absolute characteristics.

| Family / facet | Plain-language impression | Examples of notes or accords | Caveat |
|---|---|---|---|
| Citrus | Sparkling, tart, bright | Bergamot, lemon, mandarin, grapefruit | Some expressed citrus oils have phototoxicity considerations; follow finished-product instructions |
| Green | Crushed leaves, stems, crisp vegetation | Galbanum, violet leaf, grass | Can be sharp, bitter, soft or watery |
| Aromatic | Herbs, clean freshness | Lavender, rosemary, sage | Often found in fougère styles |
| Aquatic / marine | Air, water, mineral freshness | Marine accords, ozonic effects | Usually a constructed impression, not seawater |
| Fruity | Juicy, crisp or ripe | Pear, peach, plum, apple, blackcurrant | May not contain fruit extracts |
| Floral | Petals, bouquets, floral air | Rose, jasmine, orange blossom, iris | Floral does not mean feminine or sweet |
| Soft floral / powdery | Soft makeup, clean fabric, powder | Violet, iris, heliotrope, musks | Iris impression may come from various materials |
| White floral | Creamy, radiant, sometimes heady | Tuberose, jasmine, gardenia | Can be intensely diffusive |
| Amber | Warm, resinous, enveloping | Labdanum, benzoin, vanilla accords | Not automatically fossil amber or ambergris |
| Gourmand | Edible-like sweetness | Vanilla, caramel, chocolate, coffee, praline | Not edible; may be dry or restrained |
| Woody | Dry grain, creamy wood, forest | Cedar, sandalwood, vetiver, patchouli | Includes very different textures |
| Spicy | Warm or cool spice | Cardamom, pepper, cinnamon, clove | Can be fresh, sweet or dry |
| Leather / smoky | Suede, charred wood, smoke | Leather accords, birch-like effects, incense | Often constructed; does not imply burning or actual leather |
| Musk | Skin-like, clean laundry, soft warmth | Various musk materials | Musks are diverse; perception varies |
| Chypre | Contrasting fresh opening, floral/woody heart and mossy depth | Bergamot, labdanum, oakmoss-style accord | Modern formulas may use substitutes subject to restrictions |
| Fougère | Aromatic, herbal, clean, mossy | Lavender, coumarin, mossy materials | Historical family, not literal fern extract |

Taste axes: bright–dark, airy–dense, dry–sweet, clean–earthy, soft–assertive, familiar–unusual, intimate–diffusive. Use axes to clarify, not stereotype. Example: 'clean' could mean citrus soap, laundry musk, mineral water, fresh herbs or dry woods; ask which. 'Expensive smelling' is subjective: ask whether they mean understated, refined woods, polished florals, restrained sweetness or rich resins. 'Sexy' is a personal aesthetic, not a guarantee of attraction. 'Unisex' is a marketing convention; scent has no compulsory gender. 'Niche' generally refers to brand positioning/specialisation, not objective quality.

## 4. Material literacy
Natural materials are complex mixtures whose composition can vary by species, harvest, geography, extraction and batch. Synthetic materials may be nature-identical or novel; they can support consistency, safety goals, preservation of scarce resources and creative effects. Natural does not mean safer; synthetic does not mean inferior. Avoid unsupported environmental, ethical and sourcing claims.

Distillation uses steam/water or other distillation conditions to separate volatile material; expressed citrus oils commonly come from peel; solvent extraction may yield concretes and absolutes; CO2 extraction uses pressurised carbon dioxide and can yield profiles different from steam distillation. Extraction method, plant part and cultivar matter. A tincture is an extract in a solvent, often ethanol; a resinoid derives from resinous material by extraction. 'Oud' may refer to agarwood-derived material or an accord; verify before claiming natural oud. 'Ambergris' and amber accords are distinct; 'white musk' normally refers to a family of impressions/materials, not animal musk. Hedione (methyl dihydrojasmonate) is associated with transparent floral radiance; Iso E Super is a trade-name-associated woody-amber material family/product; ambroxide/ambroxan-like effects are ambergris-like woody-amber facets; vanillin is a vanilla-like molecule; coumarin has sweet hay/tonka associations; ionones may suggest violet/woody effects; aldehydes are a broad chemical class, not a single smell. These examples do not establish a particular formula, exact effect, or availability in TABAQ. Trade names, grades and stereoisomer distributions matter for technical questions.

## 5. Formulation and evaluation concepts
A technical conversation may cover accord balance, volatility distribution, odor thresholds, odor activity, headspace, partition coefficients, diffusion, masking, synergy, suppression, solvent compatibility, solubility, oxidation, light/heat stability, colour change, packaging compatibility, spray delivery, maceration/conditioning, batch reproducibility and sensory panels. Do not reduce perception to vapor pressure alone or predict a complete formula from a note pyramid. GC-MS can inform composition but may not establish the full recipe, stereochemistry, proportions or source on its own. GC-olfactometry, analytical standards and trained panels can complement chemical analysis. Comparative wear testing requires defined dosage, substrate, conditions, time points, blind or randomized assessment where feasible, and enough participants to assess variability. Anecdotes are not proof of objective superiority. A claim such as 'lasts 12 hours' must be tied to a documented method, result and limitations; never guarantee individual performance. No fabricated certificate, ingredient percentages, clinical tests or batch results.

## 6. Layering intelligence
Layering is the combined wearing of complementary fragrances, not necessarily premixing them in a bottle. It can change perceived balance, contrast, sweetness, warmth, freshness or intensity. Effects depend on both formulas, relative amounts, carrier, placement and time; blend perception is not a simple sum. Safe combined use must be assessed for the actual products and method. A family match alone cannot establish safety or pleasantness. General conceptual pairings: a citrus facet can contrast a sweet accord; dry woods can temper perceived sweetness in some blends; a soft floral accord can round sharp edges; resinous or spicy facets can add warmth; musks may give a skin-like impression. These are exploratory ideas only, not dosage recipes or guarantees. Do not instruct someone to mix finished TABAQ products in the bottle or add neat oils. The approved TABAQ ritual records specify exact allowed sequences, quantity, location, limits and description. If no validated record, do not improvise. Explain the difference between a curated core composition and optional modifiers only after product roles are verified. For existing customers, help them learn the approved rituals rather than pushing additional purchases.

## 7. Application, storage and safety
Use finished products only as labelled. Avoid eyes, mucosa, damaged skin and unintended uses. Avoid direct application of neat essential oils. Do not ingest fragrance. Do not claim safety for babies, pets, pregnancy, allergy or asthma; seek relevant professional advice. Fragrance allergens can occur in both natural and synthetic materials. Individual sensitivity varies, and a small home test cannot rule out allergy. If someone reports irritation, advise discontinuing use and seeking appropriate medical advice; severe symptoms including difficulty breathing or facial/throat swelling require urgent emergency care. No sales CTA. IFRA standards restrict, prohibit or specify conditions for certain materials in intended product categories; quantitative restrictions generally refer to concentration in the finished consumer product. IFRA does not itself issue product certificates. A supplier's certificate of conformity does not replace finished product safety assessment, combined-use evaluation or legal compliance. Never invent current category numbers, maximum levels or compliance statements. Keep alcohol-based/flammable fragrance away from ignition as labelled. Store according to label, generally away from direct light and heat, with packaging closed. Do not promise clothing compatibility or advise spraying fabric unless approved; some formulas may stain. Transport restrictions depend on carrier, product classification and destination. Do not guarantee shipping availability.

## 8. Comparison and buying guidance
Understand the exact version (EDT/EDP/parfum/flanker/year where relevant). Official brand description is preferred; distinguish listed notes from verified ingredients and subjective impressions from documented claims. Other customers' reviews can help but are individual opinions. Offer sampling when actually available, avoid blind-buy guarantees. Describe similarities by family/facet, not counterfeit or formula equivalence. For a gift, ask what the recipient already enjoys, dislikes or whether they prefer exploring; do not assume by gender. Respect budget. Explain total price, verified sizes, format and use; no invented reference price, per-wear cost or savings. Do not use hypothetical alternative retail prices as a comparison anchor. Don't imply premium status from concentration alone. No pressure to buy a large kit if it doesn't fit. General fragrance questions are welcome even if no sale results.
